The present (second) application has been filed by the applicant under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (hereinafter "BNSS"), seeking quashment of FIR bearing Crime No.
03 of 2025, registered at Police Station Ron, District Bhind for commission of offences under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, and all subsequent proceedings arising therefrom.

As per prosecution story, the complainant, Ankit Chaurasia, approached the Raun Police Station to report that Abhishek Verma (present applicant), had committed fraud and cheating amounting to Rs.15,20,000/-.

On 05.03.2024, Ankit agreed to purchase Ashok Leyland bus for Rs. 48,00,000/-
from Abhishek Verma (present applicant).
A written agreement was entered by Ankit to formalize the transaction.

Following this, Ankit paid NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24872 2 MCRC-30485-2025 the accused a total of Rs.12,45,000/- in multiple installments as follows:
on 05.03.2024 - Rs. 1,00,000/- via PhonePe (from Ankit's number 7610128753) on 08.03.2024 - Rs. 50,000/-
on 14.03.2024 - Rs. 10,000/-

sentences.text: These payments were made through RTGS from Ankit's SBI A/c No.41298466157 to the accused's Punjab National Bank account (4734000100068409), along with Rs.2,80,000/- in cash.
After receiving the payments, Abhishek (present applicant) handed over the bus (Chassis No. MBIPREHDXPAMN7176, Engine No. PMPZ107018, manufactured February 2022) to Ankit.

Ankit had the bus modified and prepared at a garage in Tekanpur at an additional cost of Rs.2,75,000/- which he paid through PhonePe (from his number 7610128753) to garage owner Naresh Vishwakarma (PhonePe number 9893451096).
Once the bus was ready, Ankit took it home on 15.06.2024.
For registration and documentation of the bus, Ankit sent the required papers to Abhishek (present applicant) via driver Anuruddh Singh.

Later, when Ankit contacted Abhishek (present applicant) by phone regarding the payment balance,
Abhishek (present applicant) demanded the full payment NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:24872 3 MCRC-30485-2025 upfront before delivering the bus.
Ankit explained that he had been paying in installments as agreed.
Abhishek (present applicant) refused and claimed that he had no money from anyone and would not return Ankit's money.

Despite having written proof of the payments,
Abhishek (present applicant) neither returned the money nor delivered the bus.
Ankit alleges that Abhishek Verma (present applicant) deliberately defrauded him of Rs.15,20,000/- through premeditated cheating.
On the basis of such allegation, the alleged FIR was registered the applicant.

Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted before this Court that according to the prosecution case, the complainant Ankit lodged a written complaint alleging that he had entered into an agreement for the purchase of a bus owned by the applicant for a total consideration of 48,00,000/-, and he paid 12,45,000/- in various instalments.
It is further alleged that the bus was handed over to him for repairs and overhauling, and that he incurred expenses amounting to 2,75,000/-.

Thereafter, the complainant claimed to had handed over the bus to the applicant for completion of formalities relating to ownership transfer, and the applicant, after obtaining possession, demanded the remaining sale consideration and refused to transfer ownership or refund the amount already received.

But, the true facts, however, reveal that the applicant and the complainant had executed a written agreement under which the complainant was required to pay forty-seven (47) instalments to the financing bank, and only upon clearing all such instalments was Abhishek Verma vs State Of Madhya Pradesh on 7 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/183105968/
2 he entitled to have the vehicle transferred in his name.

Contrary to this agreement, the complainant NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24872 4 MCRC-30485-2025 defaulted in paying the bank instalments and unlawfully began using the vehicle after changing its registration number.
Consequently, the applicant lodged a complaint on 24.06.2024 (Annexure P/4).
The complainant's default in payment is also reflected in the applicant's account statements for the period 13.02.2000 to 18.02.2025 (Annexure P/5).

Thereafter,
the bus was seized by the Police and was released in favour of the applicant by order of the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jalaun, dated 10.04.2025 (Annexure P/6).
It is thus evident that the present complaint has been filed as a counterblast to the lawful action taken by the applicant.

It was further submitted that the impugned FIR is a malicious attempt to convert a purely civil dispute into a criminal proceeding, thereby amounting to an abuse of the process of law and resulting in miscarriage of justice.
The complainant and the applicant were engaged in a commercial transaction involving the sale and purchase of an Ashok Leyland bus.
Payments were made in instalments as per mutual understanding, and delivery of the bus was duly effected.

Subsequently,
certain differences arose between the parties regarding the mode and schedule of payment, which are purely contractual in nature and devoid of any criminal element.

It was further submitted that the allegations made in the FIR, even if accepted in their entirety, do not disclose the commission of any cognizable offence and at the most, the facts disclose a civil dispute arising out of a contractual arrangement.
There was no dishonest or fraudulent intention at the inception of the transaction, which is an essential ingredient of the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC.

The dispute pertains solely to the NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:24872 5 MCRC-30485-2025 performance of contractual obligations and does not attract any criminal liability.

While placing reliance on the judgment of the Apex Court in the matter of State of Haryana v.
Bhajan Lal reported in AIR 1992 SC 604, it was submitted that where the dispute is essentially civil in nature, invocation of criminal jurisdiction amounts to an abuse of the process of law.

sentences.text: Similarly, in the matter of Anukul Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh [Criminal Appeal No.4250 of 2025], the Apex Court has held that criminal prosecution arising out of civil disputes constitutes misuse of the criminal process.

Further, while placing reliance in the matters of Punit Beriwala v. State (NCT of Delhi) [Criminal Appeal No.1834 of 2025] and Anudeep Singh Chauhan vs. (NCT of Delhi) &
Another [CRL.M.C. 1714/2025] decided by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court, it was submitted that where the allegations, even if accepted in full, disclose only a civil liability and not a criminal offence, continuation of criminal proceedings would amount to abuse of process.

sentences.text: It was further submitted that the FIR in question was lodged on 02.01.2025 and registered on the same day without any preliminary inquiry or verification of facts, which clearly demonstrates undue haste and lack of fair application of mind.
The investigation has been carried out only to bolster the complainant's false version, without any effort to ascertain the true facts.
The complainant himself is in default of payment to the bank and has used the vehicle without registration in his name while affixing a forged number plate.
His conduct clearly reveals mala fide intent and lack of bona fides in initiating these proceedings.

sentences.text: It was further submitted that the applicant emphatically denies all allegations of cheating or fraud and reiterates that the transaction in question is purely commercial and contractual.
Continuation of criminal proceedings would cause undue harassment to the applicant and amount to gross miscarriage of justice.
It is now a well-recognized tendency in commercial dealings to convert civil disputes into criminal cases merely to exert pressure upon the opposite party.
Such practice has been repeatedly deprecated by the Courts as it clogs the criminal justice system and results in injustice.
The present case is a clear instance of such misuse.

In view of the foregoing facts and legal submissions, it is prayed that the present applicaton be allowed and the impugned FIR dated 02.01.2025 and all subsequent proceedings arising therefrom,
be quashed.

Per contra, learned Public Prosecutor for the State as well as the counsel for the complainant had submitted that the applicant with dishonest intention from the very inception, induced the complainant to part with 15,20,000/- on the pretext of selling an Ashok Leyland bus, but after receiving the payment, failed to deliver valid documents and later denied having received any money.

The sequence of transactions, communications, and the applicant's conduct clearly establish fraudulent inducement and deception, which satisfy the essential ingredients of cheating as defined under Sections 415 and 420 IPC.
The mere existence of a commercial transaction does not extinguish the criminal element when dishonest intent is evident.

It is settled law that civil and criminal remedies can coexist, and an FIR cannot be quashed merely because the dispute involves financial NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24872 7 MCRC-30485-2025 dealings.
It is further submitted that the FIR was lodged only after repeated requests and demands for repayment or delivery of documents were refused.
The investigation has been conducted in accordance with law, and sufficient material exists to proceed against the applicant.
The contention that the matter is civil in nature is a deliberate attempt to escape liability.
The powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. are to be exercised sparingly and only when no offence is disclosed, which is not the case herein.
The allegations prima facie constitute a cognizable offence of cheating, and quashing the FIR at this stage would amount to interference with the due process of justice.
Hence, the application is liable to be dismissed, and the investigation and prosecution should be allowed to continue in accordance with law.
Having heard the learned counsel for both sides and perused the record.
The dispute between the applicant, Abhishek Verma, and the complainant, Ankit Chaurasia, arises out of a commercial transaction relating to the sale and purchase of an Ashok Leyland bus.

The applicant has placed on record a written agreement (Annexure P/3), which clearly provides that the complainant was required to make forty-seven (47) instalments to the financing bank before the transfer of the vehicle could be completed in his name.
The disagreement arose solely because the complainant defaulted in paying the bank instalments and began using the vehicle without completing the payments.
Such a dispute is purely contractual and cannot be converted into a criminal offence merely because it involves payments or possession of the vehicle.

sentences.text: He received payments, allowed the bus to be modified and overhauled, and agreed to facilitate registration and transfer of ownership upon completion of the agreed instalments.

The complainant's failure to comply with the terms of the agreement, coupled with unauthorized use of the vehicle and affixation of a forged number plate, demonstrates that no inducement to cheat or defraud existed at the start,
which goes to the root of the offence under Section 420 IPC, which requires dishonest intention at inception, a fact absent here.

After the complainant defaulted in payment and misused the vehicle, the applicant lodged a complaint (Annexure P/4), resulting in police seizure of the bus, which was subsequently released in his favour by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jalaun (Annexure P/6).

The FIR in question was lodged without preliminary verification of facts, indicating undue haste and mala fide intent, and amounts to abuse of the criminal process aimed at coercing the applicant into conceding the disputed amount.

Even if the allegations in the FIR are accepted at their highest, the essential ingredients of Section 420 IPC dishonest inducement, fraudulent intention, and cheating at the inception of the contract are not made out.
The applicant's conduct throughout the transaction was consistent with the contractual arrangement, and the dispute arose solely due to the complainant's non-compliance with the agreed terms.
Documentary evidence, including bank statements and the written agreement, clearly demonstrates that the allegations are groundless in law and fact.

Reliance placed by learned counsel for the applicant in the matter of State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal ( supra), Anukul Singh v. State of U.P., Punit Beriwala v. State (NCT of Delhi) [ supra], and Anudeep Singh Chauhan v. NCT of Delhi [supra], establishes that criminal proceedings cannot be invoked to resolve purely civil disputes, and the courts have the power to quash FIRs where no cognizable offence is disclosed.

sentences.text: The present matter squarely falls within this category.
Allowing continuation of criminal proceedings would cause undue harassment, result in wasteful litigation, and clog the criminal justice system.
The dispute is purely contractual, and quashing the FIR ensures that the criminal process is not misused to enforce civil claims or exert undue pressure.

Accordingly, this Court is of the considered opinion that the FIR bearing Crime No.03 of 2025,
registered at Police Station Ron, District Bhind for commission of offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, and all subsequent proceedings arising therefrom are hereby quashed.
The present application is allowed accordingly.
